column4: Righteousness includes giving wealth despite loving it to relatives, orphans, the needy, travelers, askers, and captives, making release of valued property the proof of faith.
The answer about what to spend is the surplus beyond need, directly bringing adequacy and excess into the measure of giving.
Believers must spend from their provision before a day on which trade, friendship, and intercession cannot supply what was withheld.
Spending in God's way is pictured as one seed yielding seven hundred grains, reversing the miser's arithmetic of loss and gain.
Those who spend without following the gift by reminders or injury receive their reward from their Lord, separating giving from a claim upon its recipient.
A kind word and forgiveness are better than charity followed by hurt, and God's being Rich closes a warning against transactional giving.
God erases usury and causes charities to grow, reversing the apparent financial increase of taking and decrease of giving.
The accusation that God's hand is chained is answered by His hands being outspread and His spending as He wills, opposing divine generosity to the closed-hand image of miserliness.
At harvest, people must give the crop's due right; this directly answers the garden owners who try to exclude the poor from acquired produce.
Wealth spent to block God's path becomes regret and ends in defeat, showing that even expenditure cannot avail when directed toward the wrong end.
They covenant that if God gives from His bounty they will give charity and become righteous, setting up the broken promise and miserliness exposed in 9:76.
The people resented only after God and His messenger enriched them from divine bounty, locating their material sufficiency in a gift they then deny.
God purchases believers' lives and wealth for the Garden, presenting surrendered possession as the exchange that endures.
Worldly abundance is likened to flourishing vegetation whose owners think it under their control just before it is cut down, a direct nonlexical scene of plenty becoming nothing.
Those who want worldly life and its adornment are paid their deeds in full within it, establishing a merely present and exhaustible return.
The seekers of worldly return in 11:15 have only fire in the hereafter and find their works void, exposing the final insufficiency of that payment.
Joseph's plan for seven years of abundant cultivation and stored grain gives a concrete scene of provision accumulated in anticipation of constriction.
Seven severe years consume what was stored during the abundant years, staging the movement from fullness to hardship almost literally.
A year of rain and pressing follows the famine, completing the scene with restored abundance after constriction.
Joseph's brothers arrive under hardship with poor merchandise and ask for full measure and charity, placing generosity precisely at the meeting of need and limited means.
The faithful must spend secretly and openly before a day with neither sale nor friendship, setting a deadline on wealth's useful release.
At the destroyed people's fall, what they had earned did not avail them, a concise parallel to possessions failing at ruin.
A powerless slave who owns nothing is contrasted with one given good provision who spends privately and publicly, joining possession, ability, and release in one parable.
People of means must not swear to stop giving relatives, the needy, and emigrants; pardon replaces the impulse to close the purse after injury.
Owners are told to give contracted slaves from the wealth God gave them, defining property as divine provision containing another person's route to freedom.
Long enjoyment does not avail people when the threatened punishment comes, extending the section's question from money to every benefit enjoyed before the fall.
Solomon says gratitude benefits the grateful person, while his Lord is truly Rich and Generous, relocating sufficiency from the receiver of treasure to its giver.
Creatures that do not carry their own provision are still provided for by God, countering the fear that security depends upon hoarding a store.
The question reminds people that God expands provision and restricts it, another direct formulation of the purse's fullness and emptiness under His measure.
Destroyed peoples possessed greater strength and آثار, yet what they earned did not avail them when judgment arrived.
The person seeking the hereafter's harvest receives increase, while the seeker of the worldly harvest gets only some of it and no share in the hereafter.
Neither what the condemned earned nor their protectors avail them against the waiting fire, closely matching wealth's failure at ruin.
God asks no provision from people and does not ask them to feed Him, clarifying that human giving can never be repayment of a divine need.
God alone is the Provider and possessor of firm strength, completing 51:57's denial that He needs what humans hold.
People must spend from what God has made them successors over, explicitly describing wealth as temporary custody rather than independent possession.
A good loan to God is multiplied and receives a noble reward, answering the fear that generosity only empties the hand.
People are told neither to grieve over what escapes them nor exult in what arrives, preparing the diagnosis of proud miserliness in 57:24.
The distribution rule prevents wealth from circulating only among the rich, making the social release of possessions an explicit boundary on accumulation.
The saving commerce of 61:10 consists in faith and striving with wealth and life, showing the use through which wealth can serve beyond death.
People leave the sermon for trade or amusement, but what is with God is better and God is the best provider.
Wealth and children must not distract from God's remembrance; those so distracted are named the losers before the death-regret scene of 63:10.
The ayah asks who could provide if God withheld His provision, exposing the dependence hidden by apparent self-sufficiency.
At judgment the criminal wishes to ransom himself with his own children, a direct family form of the compensation that cannot suffice.
He would offer everyone on earth if it could save him, expanding the failed ransom to the largest imaginable worldly possession.
The command to give God a good loan and send good ahead promises that it will be found with God better and greater in reward.
The condemned man is given extensive wealth, establishing the abundance that feeds his later demand for still more.
Despite extensive wealth and an eased life, he greedily desires an increase, showing that abundance has not made him inwardly sufficient.
The food of hell neither nourishes nor avails against hunger, giving the section's 'does not suffice' sense a concrete and terrible object.
The boast that one has consumed abundant wealth makes the amount spent a claim of status, immediately before the surah tests whether he took the steep path of liberating and feeding.
Failure to urge feeding the poor is a direct social form of retaining provision instead of directing it to need.
Spending wealth merely to be seen by people is set against the section's giver who seeks God's face and no human repayment.
The Lord is the truly Rich and merciful and can remove one people and appoint successors, joining divine sufficiency to the fragility of human possession.
The offer of a commerce that saves from painful punishment introduces the enduring exchange whose price in 61:11 includes wealth.
The people on the heights tell the arrogant that their gathered numbers or resources did not avail them, extending insufficiency beyond money to accumulated support.
Jacob takes prudent measures for his sons yet states that he cannot avail them at all against God, marking the boundary of even parental protection.
Those favored in provision refuse to pass it to people under their authority so that they might share equally, a social expression of treating provision as exclusively one's own.
The parable immediately before 18:46 makes worldly life vegetation that flourishes with rain and then becomes wind-scattered debris.
Moses asks not to be burdened with difficulty because of forgetfulness; this preserves the ʿusr root's ordinary sense outside the section's financial extension.
The righteous person is promised the finest reward and an easy command, another moral setting in which ease is divinely directed.
God inherits the earth and everyone upon it, supplying the ultimate ownership behind each person's abandonment of acquired goods.
God expands provision for whom He wills and measures it, repeating the section's abundance-constriction relation.
The sudden blast leaves people unable to make a bequest or return to their families, fixing the instant at which control of property and household ends.
The keys of heaven and earth belong to God, who expands and restricts provision; ownership and its changing measure meet in one formulation.
On the decisive day no protector or relation can avail another and none are helped, another interpersonal boundary on compensating for someone else.
The condemned are told that they exhausted their good things in worldly life and enjoyed them there, leaving humiliation when that enjoyment ends.
Each person's own striving is recompensed with the fullest recompense, helping distinguish divine repayment from giving in order to settle a human favor.
Neither relatives nor children benefit people on resurrection day, extending the insufficiency of possessions to the closest human bonds.
The husbands of Noah's and Lot's wives cannot avail them against God, a concrete relational instance of one person being unable to suffice for another.
The wished-for ransom expands from children to spouse and brother, showing intimate relationships treated as payments that still cannot save.
Human anxiety under harm precedes the withholding response to received good in 70:21, joining fear of constriction to the closed hand.
God says He made the man's worldly circumstances smooth and ample, supplying the ease from which the man's unsatisfied desire for increase in 74:15 arises.
People will be questioned that day about their enjoyed abundance, making worldly comfort an accountable trust rather than self-validating wealth.
